title: The Facebook–Cambridge Analytica Scandal
jurisdiction: US Federal Trade Commission (FTC) & UK Information Commissioner's Office (ICO)
summary: How personal data of up to 87 million users was harvested via third-party quiz apps and misused for political psychographic profiling.
introduction: In early 2018, whistleblowers revealed that political consulting firm Cambridge Analytica illicitly harvested profile data from up to 87 million Facebook users without their explicit consent to build voter-targeting models.
overview: The scandal originated through a personality quiz app named 'This Is Your Digital Life', developed in 2013 by researcher Aleksandr Kogan. Although only around 270,000 users installed the quiz, Facebook's Open Graph API permissions at the time allowed the app to harvest demographic, 'like', and friend-network data from all friends of those users without their knowledge or consent. This data was subsequently transferred to Cambridge Analytica in violation of Facebook's terms of service, where it was utilized to build psychographic profiles during major electoral campaigns.

timeline.description: US FTC announces unprecedented $5 billion penalty against Facebook for deceptive privacy practices.

title: The Indian Bank Phishing & Smishing Campaigns
jurisdiction: India (IT Act 2000 & Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita / IPC)
summary: How deceptive SMS notices regarding expired PAN cards and KYC updates tricked thousands into fraudulent banking clones.
introduction: Across 2021 and 2022, a coordinated wave of 'KYC suspension' SMS messages impersonating major Indian banks (SBI, HDFC, ICICI) defrauded depositors of tens of crores through cloned net-banking portals and OTP interception.
overview: Attackers leveraged bulk SMS headers and automated spoofing to transmit urgent alerts stating: 'Your bank account has been suspended due to pending PAN/KYC update. Click here to prevent account closure.' Victims clicking the embedded shortlinks landed on pixel-perfect replicas of official banking portals. Malicious JavaScript captured usernames, passwords, and secondary OTPs in real-time, instantly transmitting credentials via Telegram bots to fraudsters who triggered immediate fund exfiltration via mule accounts and UPI bridges.

title: WannaCry Ransomware Attack
jurisdiction: International Cyber Law / UK Computer Misuse Act / US CFAA
summary: A global cyberattack utilizing weaponized SMB exploits that paralyzed hospital systems, rail networks, and telecommunications in hours.
introduction: On May 12, 2017, the WannaCry cryptographic worm spread across more than 200,000 computers in 150 countries within 24 hours, crippling Britain's National Health Service, Renault, FedEx, and critical state networks.
overview: WannaCry combined ransomware payload encryption with a self-propagating network worm mechanism. It weaponized 'EternalBlue', an exploit developed by the NSA that targeted an unauthenticated remote code execution vulnerability in Microsoft's Server Message Block version 1 (SMBv1) protocol (CVE-2017-0144). Although Microsoft had released patch MS17-010 two months prior, thousands of hospitals, transport operators, and industrial enterprises had failed to patch legacy Windows installations.

title: The Instagram Data Scraping & Exposure
jurisdiction: European Union (GDPR) & Irish Data Protection Commission (DPC)
summary: How unprotected scraping databases and default business-account settings exposed contact information of millions of users including teenagers.
introduction: Between 2019 and 2021, investigative reports and regulatory inquiries revealed that contact details for millions of Instagram users—including phone numbers and email addresses of underage business-account users—were exposed to unauthorized scrapers.
overview: The vulnerability emerged from dual factors: automated web-scraping scripts abusing unprotected API endpoints, and Instagram's default profile settings for business accounts. Teenage users who transitioned their accounts to 'business' status to access platform analytics unwittingly had their phone numbers and email addresses rendered publicly visible in the page source and queryable via public API calls without age verification or privacy guardrails.

title: Celebrity Deepfake Scams & AI Voice Clones
jurisdiction: India (IT Act 2000 & IT Rules 2021) & Global Jurisdictions
summary: How hyper-realistic synthetic video and cloned audio of public figures were deployed to orchestrate viral investment scams and disinformation.
introduction: In late 2023, synthetic deepfake videos featuring Indian celebrities and business leaders (such as Sachin Tendulkar, Rashmika Mandanna, and industrialist executives) proliferated across social platforms to promote fraudulent gaming apps and fake high-yield investment schemes.
overview: Using modern deep learning and diffusion models, fraudsters generated photorealistic face-swapped video and synchronized neural voice clones. The media depicted recognizable figures endorsing unlicensed gambling portals or high-return stock schemes. The high fidelity of synthetic audio made it nearly impossible for casual viewers to discern artificial artifacts, leading to significant financial losses and reputational damage.

title: Online Harassment, Doxxing & Cyberstalking
jurisdiction: India (IT Act 2000 & Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita / IPC Section 354D)
summary: Examining targeted digital intimidation, non-consensual disclosure of personal records (doxxing), and state legal protections.
introduction: The rapid expansion of social platforms has witnessed severe escalations in digital harassment, including persistent surveillance, threatening communications, morphing photos, and doxxing (publishing home addresses and phone numbers online to incite harassment).
overview: Cyberstalking often begins with persistent unwanted messaging across multiple accounts. When blocked, perpetrators frequently resort to creating cloned profiles, publishing victim phone numbers on classified adult websites, or circulating manipulated private imagery to coerce, humiliate, or extort victims. Indian statutory law has evolved significantly to criminalize digital monitoring and privacy violations under both penal codes and cyber statutes.

title: State-Sponsored Cyber Espionage: SolarWinds Supply Chain
jurisdiction: United States Cybersecurity & Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) & International Law
summary: How sophisticated nation-state actors compromised a trusted enterprise network management software to infiltrate top government agencies.
introduction: In late 2020, security firm FireEye uncovered a catastrophic supply chain breach: Russian Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR / APT29) hackers had inserted a covert backdoor into legitimate software updates for SolarWinds Orion, a network monitoring platform used by 300,000 organizations worldwide.
overview: Rather than attacking fortified government perimeters directly, attackers targeted SolarWinds' build pipeline. By injecting malicious code ('SUNBURST') into official Orion digital updates signed with valid cryptographic certificates, the attackers established stealthy persistence inside multiple US cabinet departments (Treasury, Homeland Security, State, Defense) and Fortune 500 enterprises for over nine months undetected.

title: UPI Payment Fraud & QR Code Phishing Waves
jurisdiction: India (IT Act 2000, NPCI Guidelines & RBI Regulations)
summary: How deceptive 'Scan QR to Receive Money' tricks and fake collect requests exploited consumer misunderstandings of UPI architecture.
introduction: With the astronomical expansion of the Unified Payments Interface (UPI) across India, cybercriminals pioneered social engineering campaigns that deceptively manipulated users into entering their UPI PINs under the guise of receiving payments.
overview: A prevalent vector involves fake buyers on secondhand marketplaces (like OLX or Quikr). The scammer contacts a seller, agrees to the purchase price without bargaining, and sends a QR code or UPI 'Collect Request', falsely claiming: 'Scan this QR code and enter your PIN to accept the advance payment.' In reality, UPI architecture requires a PIN only to debit money, never to receive money. Unwitting users entering their PIN instantly authorized debits from their linked savings accounts.

title: Target Corporation Supply Chain & POS Data Breach
jurisdiction: United States (State Breach Notification Laws & FTC Act Section 5)
summary: How stolen credentials from a third-party HVAC contractor led to the compromise of 40 million credit card records during Black Friday.
introduction: During the 2013 holiday shopping season, Target Corporation suffered one of the most consequential retail breaches in history when hackers stole payment card records and personal details for over 110 million customers.
overview: The breach originated through a spear-phishing attack against Fazio Mechanical Services, a third-party heating and refrigeration contractor. Using the contractor's stolen vendor portal credentials, attackers penetrated Target's internal network, escalated privileges, traversed past insufficient network segmentation, and installed custom RAM-scraping malware ('BlackPOS') across thousands of in-store Point-of-Sale cash registers to intercept unencrypted credit card data as cards were swiped.

title: LinkedIn Credential Theft & Mass Profile Scraping
jurisdiction: United States (CFAA 18 U.S.C. § 1030 & Ninth Circuit Precedent)
summary: How scraped datasets of 700 million LinkedIn users ignited the definitive legal battle over automated scraping of publicly accessible internet data.
introduction: In mid-2021, databases containing records of approximately 700 million LinkedIn users (93% of its user base) were listed for sale on dark web hacker forums, highlighting the critical legal boundary between unauthorized hacking and automated web scraping.
overview: Unlike traditional breaches where firewalls are breached, threat actors harvested LinkedIn data by abusing official APIs and automated scraping bots that extracted public profile attributes: full names, email addresses, phone numbers, workplace histories, and social handles. This incident occurred alongside LinkedIn's landmark federal legal battle against hiQ Labs regarding whether scraping publicly visible data violates the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (CFAA).

laws.status: Seminal landmark judicial precedent limiting federal anti-hacking statute overreach.

title: Cosmos Bank Pune Malware & ATM Switch Bypass Heist
jurisdiction: India (IT Act 2000 & IPC) & International Police Cooperation (Interpol)
summary: How an international cyber syndicate bypassed a cooperative bank's ATM switch server to siphon ₹94 Crore in simultaneous ATM cash-outs across 28 nations.
introduction: In August 2018, Pune-based Cosmos Co-operative Bank was struck by one of the most audacious cyber heists in global history, losing ₹94.42 Crore ($13.5M) within hours through a coordinated malware attack on its central switching infrastructure.
overview: Attackers compromised the bank's internal network via targeted spear-phishing, planted malware, and created a rogue proxy switch server that intercepted communication between the bank's core banking system (CBS) and the payment gateway. By sending forged authorization responses, the rogue switch approved tens of thousands of cloned debit card transactions at ATMs across 28 countries (including Canada, Hong Kong, and the UK) simultaneously, followed by an illicit SWIFT transfer of ₹13.9 Crore to a bank in Hong Kong.

title: Equifax Credit Bureau Apache Struts Breach
jurisdiction: United States (FTC Act Section 5, CFPB & 50 US States)
summary: How an unpatched open-source web application vulnerability exposed credit files, Social Security Numbers, and financial histories of 147 million Americans.
introduction: In September 2017, Equifax, one of the three major credit bureaus in the United States, announced that attackers had infiltrated its dispute-portal web servers, exfiltrating the most sensitive financial and identity records of over 147 million consumers.
overview: The attackers exploited CVE-2017-5638, a critical remote code execution vulnerability in the Apache Struts web framework. Although the US-CERT had warned Equifax and released patch details in March 2017, Equifax failed to patch its external dispute resolution portal for months due to an incomplete asset inventory. Attackers gained an initial foothold, discovered unencrypted database credentials in plain text files, and queried 48 distinct databases without detection because Equifax let an internal SSL traffic-monitoring certificate expire for 19 months.

title: Twitter VIP Account Takeover & Bitcoin Scam
jurisdiction: United States (CFAA 18 U.S.C. § 1030 & Florida State Court)
summary: How phone spear-phishing (vishing) compromised internal Twitter employee tools to hijack the verified accounts of world leaders and billionaires.
introduction: On July 15, 2020, the verified Twitter accounts of Barack Obama, Joe Biden, Elon Musk, Bill Gates, Jeff Bezos, Apple, and Uber simultaneous tweeted a classic cryptocurrency double-your-money scam, generating over $118,000 in Bitcoin in minutes.
overview: The breach was accomplished not through automated software exploits, but via targeted voice phishing (vishing). A group of young hackers impersonated Twitter's internal IT helpdesk staff over telephone calls to remote-working employees, directing them to a credential-harvesting phishing site. Using the stolen credentials, they bypassed two-factor authentication and gained access to Twitter's proprietary internal administrative customer-support tool, granting them the ability to reset email addresses and seize control of high-profile accounts.

title: Colonial Pipeline Ransomware & Critical Infrastructure Shutdown
jurisdiction: United States (CIRCIA, TSA Security Directives & CISA)
summary: How a single compromised legacy VPN password brought the largest fuel pipeline in the US to an emergency shutdown, causing panic-buying across the East Coast.
introduction: On May 7, 2021, Colonial Pipeline, which supplies approximately 45% of all gasoline, diesel, and jet fuel consumed on the US East Coast, halted all pipeline operations after discovering DarkSide ransomware in its corporate IT network.
overview: Attackers breached Colonial's corporate IT network using a single compromised password for a legacy virtual private network (VPN) account that lacked multi-factor authentication. While the ransomware did not infect the Operational Technology (OT) industrial control systems that physically pump fuel, Colonial proactively halted all pipeline operations because its billing and metering software was encrypted, meaning they could not bill customers for fuel deliveries. The 6-day shutdown triggered mass fuel hoarding and state of emergency declarations across multiple states.

jurisdiction: India (IT Act 2000, CERT-In Cyber Security Directions 2022 & NCIIPC)
summary: How ransomware paralyzed outpatient registrations, lab reports, and billing systems at India's apex medical institution, forcing a two-week manual fallback.
introduction: On November 23, 2022, the All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS) in New Delhi—India's premier public referral hospital—suffered a major ransomware attack that locked down its centralized National Informatics Centre (NIC) e-Hospital servers.

Hospital staff were forced to revert to manual paper receipts, hand-written charts, and physical runners for blood test results. title: Mass Google OAuth Worm & Account Phishing Campaign
jurisdiction: United States (CFAA 18 U.S.C. § 1030) & Google Terms of Service
summary: How an abusive third-party OAuth app masquerading as 'Google Docs' spread automatically across millions of inboxes in under an hour.
introduction: On May 3, 2017, a sophisticated phishing campaign struck Google accounts worldwide. Instead of stealing passwords, the attack exploited Google's legitimate OAuth 2.0 authorization framework to grant attackers full email access without needing credentials.
overview: Victims received an invitation from a known contact saying '[Name] has shared a Google Docs document with you.' Clicking the button directed victims to Google's real authentication servers (`accounts.google.com`), where a legitimate consent prompt asked permission for an app deceptive named 'Google Docs' to access email and contacts. Once granted, the rogue application accessed the victim's address book and instantly blasted the same phishing link to all their contacts, spreading like a classic worm across millions of corporate and personal accounts.

title: SIM Swap OTP Interception & Account Takeover Wave
jurisdiction: India (IT Act 2000 & DoT Telecom KYC Rules) & US FCC
summary: How fraudsters fraudulently transfer mobile phone numbers to blank SIM cards to intercept banking OTPs and drain crypto wallets.
introduction: SIM swapping has emerged as one of the most devastating forms of identity theft, enabling attackers to hijack a victim's phone number and intercept SMS-based two-factor authentication codes to raid bank accounts, cryptocurrency wallets, and private emails.
overview: Attackers gather a victim's personal info (name, birthdate, PAN, Aadhaar) via social media or data breach dumps. They then contact the victim's mobile telecom provider or visit a retail franchise store, impersonating the victim and falsely claiming the phone was lost. Using fake identification, they trick or bribe store clerks into re-assigning the victim's phone number to a new blank SIM card in the attacker's possession. The victim's actual phone immediately loses network signal, while the attacker receives all incoming SMS OTPs and triggers password resets across financial accounts.

title: Uber Data Breach Cover-up & Bug Bounty Extortion
jurisdiction: United States (US District Court Northern District of California & FTC)
summary: How an enterprise concealed a breach of 57 million users by funneling a $100,000 ransom payment through its bug bounty program, leading to the historic federal conviction of its Chief Security Officer.
introduction: In late 2016, ride-hailing giant Uber suffered a breach exposing the names, email addresses, and driver's license numbers of 57 million users and 600,000 drivers. Instead of notifying regulators and victims, Uber's security executive paid the hackers $100,000 disguised as an ethical 'bug bounty' reward under non-disclosure agreements.
overview: Attackers discovered private AWS access keys embedded in code on Uber's GitHub repository. Using these keys, they downloaded internal customer databases. When the attackers demanded $100,000, Uber's Chief Security Officer (Joe Sullivan) arranged payment through HackerOne's bug bounty platform, requiring the hackers to sign NDAs promising never to reveal the incident. Uber failed to report the breach to the FTC—even though the FTC was actively investigating Uber for a previous 2014 data breach at that exact time.

timeline.title: Breach & Ransom Demand
timeline.description: Hackers email Uber CSO demanding six-figure payout to delete stolen database.

timeline.title: Ransom Disguised as Bounty
timeline.description: Uber pays $100,000 in Bitcoin through HackerOne bounty program; hackers sign NDAs.

timeline.title: New CEO Discloses Incident
timeline.description: Incoming CEO Dara Khosrowshahi discovers concealment, fires CSO Sullivan, and publicly reports breach.

timeline.title: CSO Criminal Conviction
timeline.description: Federal jury finds former CSO Joe Sullivan guilty of obstruction of proceedings and misprision of a felony.

topics.name: Breach Concealment & Regulatory Evasion
topics.description: Using corporate NDAs and non-disclosure mechanisms to conceal mandatory reporting events from regulators.

topics.name: Weaponization of Bug Bounty Platforms
topics.description: Distorting responsible vulnerability disclosure programs to facilitate criminal extortion payments.

topics.name: Hardcoded Credentials in Public Repositories
topics.description: Committing sensitive cloud infrastructure keys into source control environments.

laws.lawName: United States Code Title 18 (Crimes and Criminal Procedure)
laws.section: 18 U.S.C. § 1505 (Obstruction of Proceedings) & 18 U.S.C. § 4 (Misprision of Felony)
laws.explanation: Criminalizes corruptly obstructing or impeding the due administration of law before federal agencies (such as FTC) and concealing knowledge of actual felonies.
laws.incidentConnection: First time an individual Chief Information Security Officer (CISO) was criminally convicted in federal court for actions taken during incident response.
laws.status: Landmark criminal legal precedent governing C-suite cybersecurity responsibility.

laws.lawName: State Data Breach Notification Statutes (All 50 US States)
laws.explanation: Requires entities to notify affected residents without unreasonable delay when their unencrypted personal identifying info is compromised.
laws.incidentConnection: Uber settled multi-state litigation with 50 state Attorneys General for $148 million for delaying consumer notifications by over a year.
laws.status: Standardized modern state notification enforcement.

impact.label: Accounts Compromised
impact.detail: Personal details and phone numbers stolen from AWS backup clusters.

impact.label: State Settlement
impact.detail: Penalty paid by Uber to resolve nationwide multi-state attorney general investigations.

impact.label: Personal Liability
impact.detail: Federal jury conviction established that CISOs cannot legally conceal breaches from regulators.

lessons.explanation: Attempting to disguise a data breach ransom as a bug bounty is a federal crime that leads to personal criminal liability.
Use tools like GitGuardian or GitHub Secret Scanning to prevent AWS and API keys from ever being committed to code repos.
Establish independent whistleblowing and governance channels so security incidents cannot be swept under the rug.

title: Pegasus Zero-Click Spyware Surveillance Inquiry
jurisdiction: Supreme Court of India (Manohar Lal Sharma v. Union of India) & International Law
summary: How an elite commercial zero-click exploit suite compromised fully updated smartphones worldwide, triggering a landmark Supreme Court privacy and oversight ruling.
introduction: In July 2021, an international consortium of 80 journalists (the Pegasus Project) alongside Amnesty International and Citizen Lab revealed that military-grade spyware developed by Israeli firm NSO Group had targeted phones belonging to journalists, politicians, and human rights defenders globally.
overview: Pegasus represented the pinnacle of cyber weapon sophistication: a zero-click exploit that infected target devices without requiring any link-clicking or user interaction. Exploiting zero-day vulnerabilities in Apple's iMessage image parsing library ('FORCEDENTRY'), attackers could silently turn any iPhone or Android device into a 24/7 surveillance tool: exfiltrating encrypted chats (WhatsApp, Signal), accessing camera and microphone feeds, recording calls, and extracting real-time GPS locations.

timeline.title: Pegasus Project Published
timeline.description: Consortium reveals leak of 50,000 phone numbers selected as targets by NSO Group government clients.

timeline.title: Citizen Lab Discloses FORCEDENTRY
timeline.description: Researchers find zero-click PDF/iMessage exploit bypasses Apple's BlastDoor sandbox; Apple issues emergency patch.

timeline.title: Supreme Court Appoints Committee
timeline.description: Supreme Court of India forms technical expert committee headed by retired Justice R.V. Raveendran to probe allegations.

timeline.title: SC Committee Submits Report
timeline.description: Chief Justice of India notes malware was found in 5 of 29 phones examined, though conclusive Pegasus links remained inconclusive.

topics.name: Zero-Click Exploits (Zero-Interaction)
topics.description: Infecting devices through unprompted push notifications or MMS packets without user error.

topics.name: BlastDoor Sandbox Evasion
topics.description: Subverting mobile OS memory isolation layers to gain full kernel root privileges.

topics.name: State Sovereign Security vs Right to Privacy
topics.description: Balancing legitimate state counter-terrorism needs against constitutional guarantees against unlawful digital surveillance.

laws.lawName: Constitution of India & K.S. Puttaswamy (Privacy) Judgment (2017)
laws.explanation: The Supreme Court held privacy is a fundamental right. Any state surveillance must satisfy a three-fold test: legality (statutory law), necessity (legitimate aim), and proportionality.
laws.incidentConnection: Litigated in Manohar Lal Sharma v. Union of India (2021); Supreme Court emphasized that national security cannot be used as a phantom defense to avoid judicial review.
laws.status: Foundational constitutional jurisprudence on state surveillance powers in India.

laws.explanation: Section 69 permits interception of communications only through designated authorized agencies following strict statutory review committee protocols.
laws.incidentConnection: Unauthorized deployment of spyware constitutes criminal hacking under Section 43 and 66 unless carried out under valid statutory authorization.
laws.status: Strict procedural safeguards mandate periodic Home Secretary oversight.

impact.label: Infection Vector
impact.detail: Required no victim interaction, making traditional anti-phishing training ineffective.

impact.label: Surveillance Capability
impact.detail: Extracted encrypted messaging, mic recordings, cameras, and biometric credentials.

impact.label: Judicial Milestone
impact.detail: Asserted the Indian judiciary's power to review national security surveillance claims.

lessons.tip: Enable Lockdown Mode on iOS devices
lessons.explanation: Apple's Lockdown Mode blocks complex message attachment parsing and sandbox-evading vector points.
Many advanced mobile zero-days exist only in volatile memory; regular reboots force malware to re-infect.

lessons.tip: Demand strict judicial warrants for digital interception
lessons.explanation: Electronic surveillance must be bounded by independent judicial warrants and legislative oversight.

title: Aadhaar Biometric System Security & Privacy Inquiries
jurisdiction: Supreme Court of India (Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India)
summary: Examining reported database access leaks, the architectural security of the world's largest biometric identity database, and the landmark constitutional privacy ruling.
introduction: In 2018, investigative reports (notably by The Tribune) alleging that unauthorized access to the Aadhaar database portal was being sold for ₹500 over WhatsApp sparked intense national debate over biometric security, data confidentiality, and fundamental privacy rights.
overview: UIDAI maintained that core biometric data (fingerprints and iris scans) remained securely vaulted and encrypted within its Central Identities Data Repository (CIDR). However, investigative reports revealed vulnerabilities in demographic search portals and unauthorized commercial operator accounts. The controversy culminated in a historic 5-judge Constitution Bench ruling of the Supreme Court of India examining whether mandatory Aadhaar linkage violated citizens' fundamental rights.

timeline.title: Tribune Investigation Published
timeline.description: Journalist Rachna Khaira reports anonymous sellers providing demographic search portal access for ₹500.

timeline.title: UIDAI Introduces Virtual ID
timeline.description: UIDAI rolls out 16-digit Virtual IDs (VID) and Masked Aadhaar to reduce sharing of raw 12-digit numbers.

timeline.title: Landmark Supreme Court Verdict
timeline.description: 5-judge Constitution Bench upholds Aadhaar for welfare benefits, but strikes down mandatory linking for bank accounts and SIM cards.

topics.name: Biometric Data Permanence
topics.description: Unlike passwords or credit card numbers, compromised biometric identifiers cannot be reset or changed.

topics.name: Masked Aadhaar & Virtual Identity (VID)
topics.description: Using ephemeral, revocable tokens to authenticate identities without exposing permanent national ID numbers.

topics.name: Proportionality & Data Minimization
topics.description: Ensuring government identity mandates do not exceed legitimate statutory objectives.

laws.lawName: Aadhaar (Targeted Delivery of Financial Subsidies) Act, 2016
laws.explanation: Prohibits sharing core biometric information for any purpose, criminalizes unauthorized access to the CIDR with up to 3 years imprisonment and ₹10 lakh fine.
laws.incidentConnection: The legal foundation governing all Aadhaar enrollment agencies, authentication partners, and biometric vaults.
laws.status: Amended in 2019 to introduce voluntary use and strict offline verification penalties.

laws.section: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India (2019) 1 SCC 1
laws.explanation: Struck down Section 57 of the Aadhaar Act, holding that private corporations cannot mandatorily demand Aadhaar authentication for services like telecom SIMs or private bank accounts.
laws.incidentConnection: Reshaped the operational boundaries of digital identity verification in India's private sector.
laws.status: Permanent binding constitutional law of India.

impact.label: Identities Enrolled
impact.detail: World's largest digital biometric database, covering 99% of India's adult population.

impact.label: Struck Down
impact.detail: Supreme Court halted private entities from mandatorily demanding Aadhaar authentication.

impact.label: Security Innovation
impact.detail: Introduced revocable 16-digit surrogate numbers to conceal permanent identity digits.

lessons.tip: Use Masked Aadhaar instead of regular copies
lessons.explanation: Download 'Masked Aadhaar' from uidai.gov.in, which legally displays only the last 4 digits (e.g. XXXX XXXX 1234).

lessons.tip: Lock your biometrics via the mAadhaar App
lessons.explanation: Use UIDAI's Biometric Lock feature to disable fingerprint authentication until temporarily unlocked by you for transactions.
Private companies should verify customer identity via digitally signed offline XML or QR codes without storing raw numbers.
